The peak-season problem

April–August is the championship peak: the Dublin Championships, Regional Championships, Irish Open Championships and World Championships create a rush as dancers prepare for one or more events. Long first consultations take time away from design and making.

What this app changes

Families bring colour, fabric, crystal and budget ideas to the meeting. The designer develops the final dress. The demo shows how a cancelled slot could be offered to a fictional waitlist; no real alert is sent.

COUTURE SAMPLE · MADE FOR MOVEMENT

Make every peak-season design hour count

Fíor Rince is a fictional workflow prototype for an owner-operated Irish dance costume studio making bespoke solo dresses for championship dancers. Families explore colours, stocked fabric, crystals and budget before meeting the designer. This is intended to give the designer a prepared starting brief and reduce consultation time spent discovering preferences from scratch, leaving more time for design and making. The business owner is the buyer and decision-maker; designers use the system day to day to manage briefs, appointments, fittings and workload. Parents or guardians arrange the commission, while the dancer and, if invited, a teacher contribute to the brief. The prototype models how a studio could recover cancelled peak-season appointments through a sample waitlist; it does not send real alerts. All sample enquiries are fictional and based in Ireland; the designer develops every final dress.

Customer segment and problem

Specific customer: an owner-operated Irish dance costume studio making bespoke solo dresses for championship dancers, with a concentrated rush of enquiries before major competitions. Buyer/decision-maker: the studio owner. Daily user: the designer managing briefs, design appointments, fittings and collections. Parents or guardians arrange the commission; the dancer and an invited teacher can add design input.

Problem statement: Peak demand runs from April to August, around the Dublin Championships, Regional Championships, Irish Open Championships and World Championships. Dancers may need a new bespoke dress for one or more of these events. Long discovery consultations use time needed for design and making, while cancellations can leave scarce appointment time unused.

“I want each family to bring a few ideas to the consultation. If we have to start every design conversation from zero during championship season, I lose time I need to create and make the dresses.”

Invented quote for this fictional project; it is not from a real designer.

How it is handled today: families rely on costume makers’ own design and fitting processes or search for existing dresses. Elevation’s published article describes sketches, dancer feedback, fabric and embellishment choices, then fittings; it does not describe families preparing ideas before a consultation. FeisFinds is a searchable second-hand Irish-dance marketplace with filters for size, maker, condition, price and location, plus alerts for matching listings. It helps families find an existing costume, but does not brief a bespoke designer or recover a cancelled studio slot. This project tests whether a prepared design brief can save consultation time and a seasonal waitlist can recover cancellations.

What the solution must do

  • Let the family, dancer and optional teacher explore colours, stocked fabric, crystals and a sketch before the in-person consultation.
  • Show a live Basic, Premium or Supreme estimate that changes with fabric and extra crystal choices, plus the early-bird sample credit.
  • Collect the dancer’s size and sample measurements for the designer to review before the fitting.
  • Book separate design and try-on times, show availability and reminders, and give the business owner and designer a workload view.
  • On cancellation, flag the slot amber and alert the seasonal waitlist; turn it red after three unrebooked days and prevent double-booking.
  • Show the deposit and cancellation terms before the family confirms a sample booking.

Existing services already cover parts

Elevation documents parts of bespoke dress design; FeisFinds helps families search for second-hand Irish dance costumes. The two services cover design-process information and costume discovery, but do not describe a studio workflow that joins a family-prepared design brief to a booking calendar and cancelled-slot recovery. That is the combination this prototype tests. The sketch starts the conversation; the designer creates the final dress.

FeisFinds · second-hand Irish dance marketplace ↗Searches listings for second-hand Irish dance gear, including solo dresses; filters include size, maker, condition, price and location, with alerts for matching items. Checked 27 October 2026.

Reflection · draft to personalise

This project helped me focus on a busy-season problem: families may arrive at a consultation without having explored what they like, so the designer has to begin every conversation from scratch. A creative starting brief gives the family time to test ideas beforehand and gives the designer a direction to develop. A budget guide helps set the expected level of detail. The amber-to-red cancellation cue supports fast rebooking. The prototype uses fictional data and sample prices; it does not send notifications or connect to a live calendar. Before a real service, I would test the booking steps with parents and designers, confirm stock and pricing, and agree clear deposit terms.

A small studio tool for the championship rush

Solution type: a mobile-first design-start and booking portal with a calendar, cancellation tracker and studio workload view. Families prepare ideas before the consultation; designers see briefs, appointments, fittings and cancelled openings together. The designer refines the brief and creates every final dress.

1

Explore ideas before meeting

The dancer and family can mix colours, try stocked fabrics and crystal details, sketch and set a budget. A teacher can add an optional note. They bring ideas—not a finished design.

2

Refine with the designer

The family chooses a design chat and a final try-on/collection time. The designer reviews the prepared brief in the consultation, then refines the idea and confirms fit and budget.

3

Recover a cancelled slot

The Studio desk simulates an alert to the sample waitlist, tracks the opening in amber, turns it red after three unrebooked days, and blocks double-booking. No real alert is sent.

THE FOUR-WEEK COSTUME JOURNEY

A clear runway from first ideas to collection

Sample schedule · dates are confirmed by the designer. Early-bird bookings help move design work outside the championship rush.

WEEK 01

Shape the brief

Explore ideas in the app, then meet the designer to refine the design and confirm fit.

WEEK 02

Cut & create

Pattern, cut and machine-sew the costume; add the chosen fabric and crystal work.

WEEK 03

First try-on

Check movement and fit together; the designer records any requested alterations.

WEEK 04

Finish & hand over

Second try-on, final photo shoot and collection of the finished dress.

About four weeks from consultation in this fictional sample workflow; final timing depends on the design and studio capacity.
